title: The Slate Sings
passages:
The ore stub at Anza had four lamps and three of them had been dead since spring, which suited Doan fine. Their shift had ended at six and never started again — clearance withdrawn, the board said, in the flat way the board said things — so they had come out to the stub with their wrist looped twice in the overlap locker's own cord and nothing at all to do. The overlap locker was the steel box at the stub that held the key a loader used to cover two shifts at once; the latch wouldn't take their thumb anymore, so they'd taken the cord instead. A dead key was still theirs. And Doan, who had carried eleven seals' worth of somebody else's food down the ore line without once asking what the seals were for, had decided around four that morning that this was the year they asked about everything.

Then the rail started to hum. Not a chime, not a horn. Just the low note the ore line makes when something heavy comes down it slow.

It came in dark. Every rig on the Interior runs with a transponder — a box that tells the board who it is and where it is, and blinks a green lamp at the node so the yard knows to open a gate. This one had a bracket where the box should have been and nothing in the bracket but frost. It was a tender, Doan could see that much: a short rig, built to carry a crew and a water tank instead of freight. Its deck was empty and swept. No canister cradles, no receiving jaw marks, nothing on it a person could stamp.

It stopped on the stub mark without asking for a berth. Rigs chime when they want one. That's the whole arrangement. This one just sat there breathing cold.

Doan keyed the handheld. "Anza ore stub to inbound. You're dark and you're on my rails. Say a name."

The yard channel — the open channel every rig answers on when it wants something — gave back carrier hiss and nothing else.

"Great. Chatty." Doan walked a wide circle around it, cord swinging, and checked the stub reader on its post, the plate where an inbound rig says its name so the node can log it. Blank. Reader two, up in Teodoro's shop, was a different animal; that one read badges and plates and people, and Doan had no standing to be near it.

"Nour," they said into the handheld. "Ore stub. There's a tender sitting on my rails with no transponder and no post."

A pause, and the board ledge's particular silence behind her. "Then it isn't on my board and it isn't my problem."

"Bold. That's your whole personality, you know that?"

"It's kept this node eating." Another pause, and her voice came down. "Did it chime?"

"No."

"Don't touch it." Nour said it fast, the way she said things she'd already decided to be right about. "If that's coast, it's going to want a name off you, and you don't have one that's yours anymore. Get inside, Doan."

Doan looked at the empty deck, at the tank, at the swept plate where a crew should have been standing with their hands in their pockets.

"It's not coast," they said. "Coast knocks."

They put the handheld away and stood in the dark with a dead key on their wrist and did the thing they'd been avoiding since six that morning, which was think about the seals. Eleven short across four runs, all stamped Bay 4 Shift 2, all going down the line to a station that ate well. Doan had handed those canisters off and taken the roster weight for it and never asked a single question, because asking was how you lost the fat shift.

A tender with an empty deck had nothing to stamp. That was what sat wrong. Whatever this was, it hadn't come for the food.

Something inside the hull let go — a latch, heavy, unhurried. A seam of yellow light opened along the flank, and a step folded down onto the frozen stub with a sound like a dropped wrench.

Doan didn't move. "Well," they said. "Nobody ever just knocks."

The man who came down the step was broad and unhurried, in a coast coat with the storm flap taped shut at the hem, and he came with his empty hand already out.

"Coombs," he said. "Haulage contract, coast side. Don't mind the cord, friend, I've seen worse at better nodes." His grip was warm through Doan's glove. "You're the one who hailed me. I heard you. Nobody hails anymore, it's very restful."

"You didn't answer."

"I don't talk on the yard channel. Everything said on the yard channel is said twice." He reached back into the seam of light and brought out a flat gray slate, the size of a dinner plate, glass across the face and one corner worn pale by a thumb. "This does my asking. Proving slate. It reads how you walk and what comes out of your mouth when you say your own name, and it sets that against every list the coast keeps — node rosters, relay badges, contract books, the winter rolls."

Doan looked at it and did not step back, which took some doing. "And then what."

"And then it says the name back. That's all. It's a mouth, not a judge." He held it up so the dead lamp behind Doan caught in the glass. "Two things it can't do, and I want you to know them, because people get frightened of a thing they think is a judge. First, it has to see you move and hear you talk. Stand still and keep your teeth together and it's a plate of window. Second, it only ever says back what somebody already wrote down. It cannot make a man up. Never on paper, it walks you right past like weather."

"Everything's on paper somewhere," Doan said.

"Now you've got it." Coombs said it like a compliment, which was somehow worse.

A loader came across the stub with a thermos in both hands, hood up, cutting the corner by the ore chute the way people do at shift change when they want ten more minutes of sleep. The slate chimed once, soft, like a spoon on a glass.

"Morning, Salas," Coombs said. "Anza, Shift one, seal rating current."

Salas stopped dead. "It's not morning."

"It's ten past five."

"It's a *concept*, is what it is." Salas looked at Doan, then at the slate, then backed off toward the lit yard. "Doan. Don't let that thing look at you."

"I'm on a roster," Doan said.

"So was I," said Salas, and went.

Coombs watched them go with real fondness. "That's the trouble with a node. Everybody's warm and nobody's free." He turned the slate slowly, sweeping it across the swept deck, the tank, the stub reader with nothing on it, and Doan saw the glass was not blank after all — a thin crawl of gray in it, like frost forming and unforming.

"You're not on it," Doan said.

"You are, friend. Live roster, clearance pulled but the line still holds you. That's where I want everybody. Which is why I'm not pointing this at you." He kept sweeping. Past the cradles. Past the ore chute. Into the dark siding where the scrubber cradles sat in rows and the only light was what leaked off the yard.

"Doan," he said, pleasant as a man asking after a family. "How many bunks do you figure I'm carrying? Six. Water tank, stove, six bunks, and the stove stays lit from Kettering to the coast and back. I have never once had to explain to a mother why I was empty."

"That's a lot of speech for a man who won't use the radio."

"I'm a talker. It's my one vice." The slate's gray crawl thickened. Coombs's thumb settled on the worn corner and the sweep slowed, and slowed, and stopped square on the black gap between two cradles.

"There," he said, still genial, still warm, and pitched his voice past Doan into the dark like a man calling a dog he already liked. "Been walking back and forth in there since I came in. Small steps. Counting, near enough. Come on out where I can see you, and I'll say your name nice."

The dark didn't take the invitation. Miko took it instead, coming out of the gap between the cradles sideways, a coil of seal clip riding one hip, hood shoved back, chin already up like she was walking into an argument she'd started herself.

The slate chimed.

"Dalia Reyes," Coombs said, warm as a man reading a child's marks. "Coast contract book, filed nine days back. Passage paid, Kettering to the coast, one berth, no return leg. Not on a single Anza roster, but the coast wrote it down and took the money, so it's real." He tipped the glass toward the yard. "First honest thing I've read all week."

"That's a bold read of a stolen name," Miko said.

"It's not stolen, it's *bought*, there's a difference and the difference is a receipt." Coombs let the slate drop to his side. "And I don't care about the name, Dalia. Nobody honest has one worth reading. What I care about is the berth, because a paid berth on a green board is the loneliest thing on the Interior. The train runs and doesn't stop, because your name's on the load and not on the crew, and you spend the whole ride watching your own reflection in a window that isn't going to open."

Doan, from the locker, cord swinging: "Ask him about the bunks."

"I was *getting* to the bunks," Miko said.

"Six of them," Coombs said. "Water tank, stove lit Kettering to the coast and—"

"You already ran that." Miko pointed the coil of clip at him, one loop sliding free. "Word for word. To the cord kid. Six bunks, the tank, the stove, and the bit about your mother. I heard the whole hymn from the cradles."

Coombs had the grace to look pleased rather than caught. "It's a good hymn."

"It's a *recycled* hymn." She let another loop of clip fall. "What's the verse you skipped? The one where the logged wage shows up, because I notice you sang the whole first chorus and stopped right before the money."

Doan made a small sound at the locker, the sound of someone revising an estimate upward.

"There it is," Coombs said, and something in him settled, the genial thing turning practical underneath. "You've done this before. Fine. The wage's real. Logged at the far end, a coast number, spendable in a town with a door on it, not scrip, not roster weight. That's the verse. And here's the rest of it, since you asked straight: I carry the count too. Whatever the slate read off you, whatever a desk at Kettering has filed, it goes in and it comes out clean. Not hidden. *Wiped.* You step on my deck as Dalia Reyes and step off as whoever's left when you're sick of her, and no morning desk from here to the water has a line on you."

Miko stopped fidgeting with the clip. That one had landed, and she didn't bother hiding that it had. "Do the bunks have doors."

"Curtains."

"A curtain's a door for people who've never been robbed."

"Twice," Coombs agreed. "Both times by someone I liked." He didn't push. That was the trick of him — he let the pitch sit there in the cold and let her look at it. "Take your time. Stove's not going anywhere and neither am I."

Miko took a step. Not toward the yard. Toward the slate, into the middle of the one live lamp, arms loose, chin working, buying seconds with her body the way she'd buy them with her mouth. "How many runners off Anza this year?"

"Four. Two of them write to me. Badly."

"Fuel on the stove?"

"Enough. I melt more at the Weir."

"And if I said no?"

"Then you said no, and I'd be sorry, and the cold would keep arguing my side for me." He said it without any weight at all, which was the weight of it.

She kept talking — the tank, the water, how long the trestle stop ran — and kept drifting, putting herself square in the glass's path so the gray crawl in it had to cross her to reach anything past her, and thinned as it went.

"You're in my light, Dalia."

"It's Anza's light."

The slate chimed a second time. Pointed at the black gap. Nothing in the lamplight, nothing but two cradles and a wall.

Miko stopped mid-word, mouth still open.

Coombs didn't turn his head. "That one," he said, "is shy."
